attribution.note: Zitron says in his own words that inflating revenue this way is 'exactly what OpenAI is doing'. He cites unnamed sources, but the allegation is his own and he endorses it.

semantics.note: Faithful: a present-tense allegation that OpenAI uses busy four-week windows to inflate annualized revenue. The product launch is only an example.

contract.note: The plain reading (deliberately choosing or timing unrepresentative windows) is the ordinary meaning of 'inflate'. The March–August 2026 period is reasonable. The contract is fair and does not decide the result.

evidence.note: Secondary summary from March 2026. It says the short window makes the run rate sensitive to recent spending. That is sensitivity, not proof of deliberate selection or disproof of it.

reviews.rationale: The only admitted item shows that the four-week metric is sensitive. It does not show that OpenAI chose windows or timed disclosures to overstate its run rate, and it does not show consistent practice either. No weekly revenue or disclosure records were obtained, so the allegation is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own analytical statement in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Keeps the revenue-acceleration antecedent and the firm 'will need several more $122 billion rounds'. The 'dwindling' investor-capital clause is kept.

contract.note: Reading 'several' as at least three is the drafter's own choice and is flagged as such. It is a reasonable, ordinary reading and has no effect while the antecedent is unestablished.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own September 2026 disclosure of a 20% cut in serving costs. It is a company claim about unit cost, not total costs. It does not establish revenue acceleration or financing need.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent (revenue growth accelerating after publication) is not established by any admitted evidence, so the conditional cannot be scored. No deadline was stated and no conclusive event appears. The serving-cost disclosure is context only.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The proposition is faithful. The stored 'antecedent' is really a purpose clause. The effective conditional is: if OpenAI exits 2026 well below ~$75B annualized, it essentially cannot pay its compute costs. 'Snowball's chance' is firm hyperbole, not a hedge.

contract.note: Checking year-end annualized revenue, and then whether obligations get paid, is a fair reading of the necessity claim. Allowing a tolerance around 'in the region of' is fair to the speaker.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own March 31, 2026 announcement of a $122B committed round. It predates the statement and does not show year-end cash or coverage of compute obligations, so it does not meet the early-resolution rule.

reviews.rationale: The revenue checkpoint is December 31, 2026, after the evaluation date. No binding arrangement in the packet shows that the compute obligations can be paid without the threshold, so the early-resolution rule is not met. The claim is not yet due.

attribution.note: Zitron's own forecast, drawn from the Bloomberg report he quotes. The forecast itself is his.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'if' antecedent and the firm 'going to have' trouble. Leaving out the CEO description is fine; it is descriptive, not an outcome.

contract.note: Reading the claim as private-credit funds struggling to raise investor money for OpenAI matches his words. Treating general equity rounds as context is reasonable. The 'substantial difficulty' markers are an ordinary reading.

evidence.note: Bloomberg, reproduced by Bankwatch, before publication. It reports slow progress and no signed deals, which bears only on the antecedent and only partly: debt-investor concern later eased, and the deals were chip financing. It is not evidence of the outcome.

CNBC, October 2026: OpenAI nearing an equity round of up to $30B led by UAE investors and Coatue, with investors approaching OpenAI first. This is a counterpoint, but the round is not complete and is not private-credit financing.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent has at best limited support. No completed or abandoned OpenAI fundraising through private-credit funds is documented, and nothing shows either substantial difficulty or strong demand. The October equity round is unfinished and outside the claim's channel. No deadline was stated, so the forecast is unresolved.
